meta.title: The High Routes
meta.description: High Route 1 of the Giants and High Route 2 of the Shepherds: the official multi-day routes of Aosta Valley with stage data and maps.

AlteVie.heroEyebrow: Official routes — Aosta Valley Autonomous Region
AlteVie.heroSubtitle: The High Routes are the official multi-day itineraries of Aosta Valley: waymarked regional routes crossing the region from east to west, linking Walser villages, historic refuges and cols above 2,700 m. Unlike Tours — loops around a single massif — the High Routes tell the full story of the Aosta Valley in one traverse. Born in the 1970s as a hiking alternative to mass tourism, they remain among the most complete alpine treks in Europe, with a refuge network, CAI waymarking and official data from the regional trail registry.
AlteVie.mapHint: Official VdA Region GPX tracks · use zoom and compass to explore
AlteVie.compareSubtitle: AV1 crosses the three great massifs on the northern flank; AV2 follows the southern side with a naturalist focus and Gran Paradiso wildlife.

av1.name: High Route 1 — of the Giants
av1.description: High Route 1 crosses the entire Aosta Valley, touching all three great massifs — Monte Rosa, Matterhorn and Mont Blanc — in seventeen stages from the vineyards of Donnas (322 m) to the ridges above Courmayeur. It is the most complete alpine traverse in the region: Walser pastures, glacial lakes, historic refuges and panoramas from Gran Paradiso to Mont Blanc. Created in the 1970s as a hiking alternative to mountaineering routes, it is now the most popular multi-day route in the valley, with impeccable waymarking and a well-distributed refuge network. This site covers all 17 stages with GPX, elevation profiles, geology and verified practical data.

av2.name: High Route 2 — Naturalistica
av2.route: Courmayeur → Donnas (southern flank, right orographic bank)
av2.description: The Naturalistica High Route crosses the southern flank of Aosta Valley — Val Veny, La Thuile, Valgrisenche, Rhêmes, Valsavarenche, Cogne and Champorcher — with outstanding wildlife in Gran Paradiso and Mont Avic parks. First section of the Tor des Géants route. This site covers all 14 stages with data verified from lovevda.it and the official trail registry.
av2.sources: Sources: lovevda.it, VdA Trail Registry, Wikipedia

AlteVie.legalNote: High Routes 1 and 2 are official waymarked routes of the Aosta Valley Autonomous Region. The numbering (AV1, AV2) is official. Massif Tours (TMB, Tour Monte Rosa, etc.) are distinct routes listed in the <tourLink>Tours section</tourLink>.

meta.title: The Tours
meta.description: Tour of Mont Blanc, Monte Rosa, Matterhorn, Gran Paradiso, Rutor and Grand Combin: hiking loops around the great Aosta Valley massifs.

Tour.heroSubtitle: Tours are hiking loops circling a massif, often crossing borders and multiple valleys. Unlike High Routes — which traverse Aosta Valley from east to west — Tours follow the rim of a single mountain group. The Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB) is the world's most famous; other Valdostan routes offer wilder, quieter alternatives around Rosa, Matterhorn, Gran Paradiso, Rutor and Grand Combin.
Tour.mapHint: Official GPX tracks · use zoom and compass to explore

tmb.name: Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB)
tmb.places: Courmayeur, Rif. Bertone (2,011 m), Rif. Bonatti (2,025 m), Rif. Elena (2,062 m), La Fouly (CH)
tmb.description: The most famous route in the Alps: ten full days, three countries, constant views of the south face of Mont Blanc. The Italian section in Val Ferret — from Courmayeur to Rifugio Bonatti — is considered the most spectacular on the entire loop, with Grandes Jorasses and the Miage glacier.

monteRosa.name: Tour of Monte Rosa
monteRosa.description: A loop around the second highest massif in the Alps, crossing Walser valleys, Lys glaciers and passes above 2,700 m. The Valdostan section links Gressoney, Ayas and Valsesia in a route less crowded than the TMB but equally grand.

cervino.name: Tour of the Matterhorn
cervino.description: Circles the most iconic pyramid in the Alps, alternating Italian and Swiss valleys. The Valdostan side offers Plateau Rosa, huts above Valtournenche and head-on Matterhorn views matched by few other trails.

granParadiso.name: Tour of Gran Paradiso
granParadiso.description: A loop entirely within Gran Paradiso National Park: Cogne, Valsavarenche and Valle dell'Orco (Piedmont). Outstanding wildlife — ibex almost guaranteed — and a landscape studied by glaciologists as a laboratory of alpine climate change.

rutor.name: Tour of Rutor
rutor.description: One of the lesser-known tours but among the most accessible for observing an active glacier. The loop around Rutor, above La Thuile, combines quiet summer farms, glacial lakes and views of the western Mont Blanc massif.

granCombin.name: Tour of Grand Combin
granCombin.description: A massif less known to the general public but glaciologically spectacular: the cross-border loop crosses Valpelline and the Swiss side with passes above 2,700 m and views of Combin de Grafeneire.

meta.title: The project
meta.description: Sentieri VdA: a 360° editorial guide to trails, environment and culture in Aosta Valley.

Progetto.heroSubtitle: Trails, environment, nature and Valdostan culture — with verified data and editorial depth.
Progetto.intro: Sentieri VdA offers an integrated view of the Valdostan alpine territory: not just a list of routes, but a navigable atlas linking every stage to landscape, geology, wildlife and cultural roots.
Progetto.mission: The goal is to build the most complete resource on Aosta Valley trails — from High Routes to tours around the great massifs, from huts to summits, from natural environment to Walser culture and food — with verifiable information and no invented data.
Progetto.pillarTrailsBody: Full pages with GPX, elevation profiles, CAI grades, refuges and warnings. Data from the Region's official trail registry.
Progetto.pillarAmbienteBody: Massifs with in-depth pages and 3D views, geology, hydrology, glaciers and 4,000 m peaks.
Progetto.pillarNatureBody: Catalogued species with photos, ranges and links to trails where they can be observed.
Progetto.pillarCultureBody: Valleys, traditions, food and wine and historic villages along High Routes and tours.
Progetto.dataBody: Trail data comes exclusively from the Aosta Valley Region's Catasto Sentieri, OpenStreetMap and verified CAI sources. Descriptions are original; photos are attributed. Independent project, no sponsors.
Progetto.authorBio: Hiker and Aosta Valley mountain enthusiast. Every trail page cross-checks official data, GPX tracks and field notes. No invented figures: if something cannot be verified, it stays empty.

meta.title: How we verify data
meta.description: Official sources — Catasto Sentieri VdA, OpenStreetMap and Geoportale: Sentieri VdA's editorial method and last-verified date on every trail page.

Metodo.heroSubtitle: Every trail page shows its official source and last verified date. Here is where the numbers come from and how we check them.
Metodo.intro: Sentieri VdA is an independent editorial project. We do not invent distances, elevations or grades: we use only traceable data and leave fields empty when they cannot be verified. Narrative descriptions are original but grounded in institutional and open data sources.
Metodo.sctBody: Primary source for trail code, name, municipality, length, start/end elevation, CAI grade and official network geometry (~5,000 km). Open data licence DGR 899/2014. Updated periodically via regional WFS/GeoJSON.
Metodo.osmBody: Used to fill missing GPX tracks, toponyms and points of interest along routes. OSM is crowd-sourced: we treat it as a complement, not the sole source for distance or difficulty.
Metodo.geoBody: Official trail network package (shapefile/KMZ) and cartographic metadata from the Aosta Valley Region. Used to validate geometries and compare dataset versions.
Metodo.verifyBody: Every curated page in trails.json includes updated_at: the date when distance, elevation, grade and GPX were checked or refreshed. You will find it at the bottom of each trail page, next to the data source.
Metodo.verifyNote: Trails change: landslides, late snow, diversions. Always check current conditions on the official registry or at the nearest refuge before setting out.

meta.title: Mountain safety
meta.description: Equipment, weather, mountain rescue and useful contacts before setting out in Aosta Valley.

Sicurezza.heroSubtitle: Before you set foot on the trail: check conditions, read the weather, pack your bag and know what to do in an emergency. Mountain safety starts before you leave.
Sicurezza.emergencyBody: 118 is Italy's single emergency medical number. It works 24/7, is free and answers even without phone credit. In Aosta Valley, 118 calls can activate the Soccorso Alpino Valdostano (SAV) — the specialist team for mountain, trail and high-altitude rescue.
Sicurezza.emergencyExtra: Before calling, make yourself and others safe. With no signal, use the international distress signal: 6 visual or acoustic signals per minute (whistle, torch, mirror, shouts), then pause one minute, repeated until spotted. Staying visible in one place is usually faster to find than moving without orientation.
Sicurezza.responsibilityBody: No website, map or trail page replaces what you see on the ground. Sentieri VdA uses official sources, but landslides, late snow, removed bridges and diversions can change a route overnight. The final decision to start, continue or turn back is always yours.
responsibilityPoints: Check updated conditions on lovevda.it or Catasto Sentieri VdA the day before and on the morning of your hike
Ask the nearest hut, CAI section or village — they often know of ice or landslides not yet online
Choose the route for the weakest member of the group, not the most experienced
Tell someone your route, expected return time and when to worry if they don't hear from you
Skip the summit or long loop if weather, snow, fatigue or missing signs require it — turning back is the right call
Sicurezza.equipmentIntro: CAI grade describes the route, not what to carry. On an E (Hiker) trail, treat the list below as a minimum. On EE/EEA add helmet, crampons or ice axe by season, and climbing gear only if the route requires it.
Sicurezza.equipmentNote: In Aosta Valley elevation changes fast: you may start at 600 m in a T-shirt and find snow or strong wind above 2,500 m. Pack for the highest point of the route, not valley temperature.
equipmentItems: Trekking boots with Vibram sole and ankle support — grip matters on wet rock and scree
Layered clothing: thermal base, fleece, waterproof windproof shell
At least 1.5 L water per person in summer; more in heat or if no reliable springs
Emergency food (bars, nuts): delays from weather or fatigue are common
1:25,000 map or offline app with GPX — mobile coverage is often missing in side valleys
Charged phone, power bank if possible, with 118 saved in contacts
First-aid kit: plasters, bandage, antiseptic, emergency blanket
Trekking poles on routes with significant elevation gain
High-factor sunscreen and sunglasses — UV increases quickly with altitude
Headlamp if starting in the dark or returning after sunset
Light thermal layer even in summer above 2,200–2,500 m
Sicurezza.weatherBody: Mountain weather differs from the valley floor. Check forecasts for the 24 hours before departure, using sources that show altitude and aspect. In Aosta Valley use ARPA VdA and Fondazione Montagna Sicura; for the French border (Mont Blanc, Val Ferret, Val Veny) add Météo France. Summer afternoon storms above 2,000 m are common — cumulus building to the west is often visible hours ahead.
weatherPoints: Start early: if the sky looks unstable, aim to be below 2,400 m by 1 pm
Do not stay on exposed ridges, below cliffs or in gullies when clouds build — lightning seeks high points
In winter and spring check the avalanche bulletin before leaving marked trails
Snow can last until June–July on north slopes and passes above 2,500 m — verify on the ground
Wind on ridges lowers perceived temperature sharply — always carry a windproof layer
If weather worsens, the safest choice is to shorten the route or turn back, not speed up

Sicurezza.signalsIntro: In the mountains, danger signs appear before a situation becomes critical. Learning to read them keeps you from getting into trouble at altitude or far from the nearest hut. If you notice one, the safest choice is almost always to turn back or shorten the route — skipping a summit is not a failure.
signalItems: Sky darkening to the west with rapidly growing cumulus — afternoon storm likely
Temperature drop and rising wind even in summer — deterioration at altitude
Trail covered by soft snow, ice or fresh debris — assess whether you have suitable gear
Missing, damaged or ignored closure signs — do not continue blindly
Excessive fatigue, dizziness, nausea or pounding headache — possible altitude sickness (AMS)
Cracking or moving snow on steep slopes — avalanche risk, move away from the slope
Recent landslide or damaged bridge/section — ground may still be unstable
Sicurezza.rescueIntro: In an accident, first protect the injured from cold and rock fall, then call 118. The operator activates the SAV and guides you step by step — answer calmly even if the line is poor. Do not hang up; they may call back for details.
Sicurezza.rescueNote: Without phone signal, send GPS coordinates to a trusted contact (WhatsApp, SMS) and stay as visible as possible — bright clothing, arm movements. In a group, one person stays with the injured while others seek signal. Never leave an injured person alone without care.
rescueSteps: Caller: full name, phone number, relationship to the group
Location: trail name, nearest hut or village, approximate altitude, GPS coordinates if available
What happened: number of people, type of injury (fall, lost, illness, hypothermia)
On-site conditions: conscious or not, mobile or trapped, current weather and visibility
Signal: if the line is unstable, say so immediately so they record essentials
Sicurezza.familyBody: On the trail, good practice protects hikers, those who follow and the mountain environment. Aosta Valley has protected parks, active pastures and shared routes with climbers and bikers — respecting signs and etiquette reduces avoidable incidents.
familyPoints: Respect closure signs, diversions and fences — they often mark landslides, hunting or works
In Gran Paradiso National Park dogs must be on lead on all routes
In pastures with livestock keep dogs on a short lead and do not cross fences
With children choose T routes, plan frequent breaks and extra layers — they cool down faster
Leave no litter, do not cut unmarked shortcuts, no fires outside designated areas
On narrow or uphill sections give way to those climbing — slow down and greet
Do not disturb wildlife — observe from a distance, especially ibex and chamois in breeding season
Sicurezza.contactsSubtitle: Save these links and numbers before you leave, especially on routes without coverage. Use official sources for trail conditions; check ARPA and Fondazione Montagna Sicura for weather and avalanches on the day of your hike.
